title: From Python functions to HTTP responses
outcome: Trace a request through routing, a handler and a response using two real in-process client requests.

key_terms.HTTP request: A client message made of a method such as GET, a target such as `/greet/Ada`, headers and an optional body.
key_terms.Route: A registered pairing of an HTTP method and a URL pattern with the view function that handles matching requests.
key_terms.View function: The Python function a route invokes to turn one request into a response, here returning a dictionary and a status code.
key_terms.Status code: The three-digit number in a response that reports the outcome, such as 200 for success or 404 when no route matches.
key_terms.Test client: A framework helper that sends requests through the real application in process, without a TCP listener, TLS or a browser.

worked_examples.title: a direct call versus a routed request
worked_examples.interpretation: The first line is a plain Python tuple: calling `greet("Ada")` never touches routing, so nothing turned the dictionary into JSON or chose a media type. The second line went through the registered GET rule, and Flask converted the same dictionary into a response with status 200, an `application/json` header and a decodable body. The third request uses POST on a path that only has a GET rule, so the router answers 405 Method Not Allowed before `greet` runs; change the decorator to `@app.route("/greet/<name>", methods=["GET", "POST"])` and that line would print 200 instead, because the same view would then accept both methods.

title: URLs, path parameters and query strings
outcome: Distinguish resource paths, repeated query values, percent encoding and missing-route behavior.

key_terms.Path parameter: A variable segment of a route pattern, such as `<name>`, that the router decodes and passes to the handler as an argument.
key_terms.Query string: The part of a URL after `?` that carries `key=value` options; Flask exposes the parsed values through `request.args`.
key_terms.Percent encoding: The URL convention that writes a byte as `%` plus two hexadecimal digits, so `%20` represents a space in `/people/Ada%20Lovelace`.
key_terms.Multidict: A mapping that can keep several values under one key, so `getlist("tag")` returns every `tag` value while a single lookup returns one.
key_terms.Path converter: A route rule such as `<int:item_id>` that restricts which segments match and converts the match to a Python value; a nonmatching segment produces 404 Not Found.

worked_examples.title: reading the same URL three ways
worked_examples.interpretation: The router decoded `%20` before the handler saw `name`, so the view received `Grace Hopper` with a real space. The query string held two `tag` values: `get` returned only `navy`, while `getlist` kept both in order, which is the difference between a single option and a repeated filter. The `page=x` value failed the `type=int` conversion, so Flask silently used the default `1`; that is convenient for optional paging but would hide a client mistake if you needed an explicit 400. The second request shows that a literal slash is a path separator: `<name>` matches one segment only, so `/people/Grace/Hopper` finds no rule and returns 404. Using `<path:name>` would accept it.

title: HTTP methods, status codes and idempotence
outcome: Compare repeated replacement and deletion operations without confusing equal effects with equal status codes.

key_terms.Safe method: A method such as GET whose intended semantics are read-only from the client's perspective, even if the server records logs or metrics.
key_terms.Idempotent method: A method whose intended effect after several identical requests equals the effect of one request, as with PUT replacement and DELETE removal.
key_terms.PUT: A method that stores the complete representation in the request body at the target URL; this example returns 201 when it creates and 200 when it replaces.
key_terms.DELETE: A method that removes the target resource; here the first request returns 204 and a repeat returns 404 while the final state stays absent.
key_terms.204 No Content: A success status meaning the server fulfilled the request and intentionally sends no response body.

worked_examples.title: PUT is idempotent but POST is not
worked_examples.interpretation: Sending the same PUT three times left exactly one record at key 5: the first call created it (201) and the repeats replaced it with an identical value (200). The statuses differ, yet the server state after one call equals the state after three, which is what idempotence means. The POST loop is the contrast: each identical body allocated a fresh identifier, so three retries produced records 6, 7 and 8. A client that retries a timed-out POST can therefore duplicate data, while retrying this PUT is safe. If the PUT handler appended to a list instead of assigning `records[item_id]`, it would stop being idempotent even though the method name stayed PUT.

title: Headers, JSON, bytes and content negotiation
outcome: Validate media types and Unicode representations and diagnose malformed request bodies.

key_terms.Content-Type: The header that declares the media type of the body being sent, such as `application/json`, so the receiver knows how to parse it.
key_terms.Accept: The request header listing media types the client is willing to receive in the response, a different question from the body's Content-Type.
key_terms.415 Unsupported Media Type: The status a server returns when the request body is declared in a media type the endpoint does not process.
key_terms.UTF-8: A variable-length encoding of Unicode code points into bytes; `"café"` has four code points but five UTF-8 bytes.
key_terms.Content negotiation: Selecting a response representation from client preferences such as Accept; this endpoint documents one format instead of implementing full quality-weighted negotiation.

worked_examples.title: characters, bytes and the Content-Type header
worked_examples.interpretation: Both requests carried the identical 18 bytes: `{"text": "naïve"}` is 17 characters, but `ï` takes two bytes in UTF-8. Only the header changed, and that alone decided whether `request.is_json` was true. The server did not sniff the payload; it trusted the declared media type, which is why the lesson's handler returns 415 for `text/plain`. Counting `len(raw)` measures bytes on the wire, while `len("naïve")` would report 5 characters, so size limits and character limits are different checks. If you encoded with `ensure_ascii=True` the body would contain `\u00ef` instead, grow to 22 bytes and still decode to the same Python string.

title: Input schemas and explicit validation errors
outcome: Reject ambiguous coercions and unexpected fields with an explained structured error contract.

key_terms.Input schema: A declared contract for incoming data listing required fields, allowed types, bounds and the treatment of unknown fields, here the Pydantic `Order` model.
key_terms.Type coercion: Automatically converting a value of one type into another, such as the string `"3"` into the integer 3, which strict validation refuses.
key_terms.Strict mode: The Pydantic setting `strict=True`, which rejects inputs that would need coercion, so neither a string nor the boolean `True` becomes an integer quantity.
key_terms.Extra-field rejection: The `extra="forbid"` policy that reports any field outside the model, such as `approved`, instead of silently ignoring or assigning it.
key_terms.422 Unprocessable Content: The status for a request whose body parsed correctly but whose content fails validation; this endpoint lists the failing field paths and error types.

worked_examples.title: strict and lax validation of the same payload
code: from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict, Field, ValidationError
print([(e["loc"], e["type"]) for e in error.errors()])
worked_examples.interpretation: The lax model accepted the string `"3"` by coercing it to the integer 3 and silently dropped the unknown `note` field, so the client never learns that its gift note was ignored. The strict model, configured like the lesson's `Order`, reported two separate problems with machine-readable locations: `quantity` had the wrong JSON type and `note` was not part of the contract. Those `loc` and `type` values are exactly what the lesson's 422 response copies into its `errors` list. If the payload sent `"quantity": 30` as a real integer, the strict model would instead report `less_than_equal` because the type passed but the `le=10` bound failed.

title: HTML templates and context-aware escaping
outcome: Render untrusted text safely and separate escaping from validating a URL or trusted HTML fragment.

key_terms.Jinja template: A text file with placeholders and control statements that Flask renders into HTML by inserting values from the view.
key_terms.Autoescaping: A template setting that converts characters such as `<`, `>` and `&` in inserted values into HTML entities so the browser displays them as text.
key_terms.Markup: A string type that tells Jinja a value is trusted HTML and must not be escaped; only author-owned constants should receive it.
key_terms.Output context: The place a value is inserted, such as HTML text, an attribute, JavaScript, CSS or a URL, each with its own interpretation and escaping rules.
key_terms.Destination allowlist: A fixed mapping from accepted names to known local paths, used instead of treating a client-supplied string as a ready-to-use URL.

worked_examples.title: where autoescaping applies and where it does not
worked_examples.interpretation: Jinja escaped the hostile title in the element body and inside a quoted attribute, turning `"`, `<` and `>` into entities so the browser would display the text instead of building an `img` element. The middle line shows the cost of `|safe`: the filter marks the value as trusted markup, so the injected tag is emitted verbatim and would run its `onerror` handler. That is why the lesson only wraps a fixed, author-owned literal in `Markup`. Escaping still does not make a URL safe: a value such as `javascript:alert(1)` contains no characters to escape, so placing it in `href` would remain dangerous, which is the reason the lesson maps destination names to an allowlist of paths.

title: Forms, multipart data and upload limits
outcome: Parse form and file requests, enforce size and content contracts and keep filenames out of trusted paths.

key_terms.multipart/form-data: A request encoding that splits the body into parts so text fields and uploaded file bytes can travel in one request.
key_terms.Repeated form field: A form field name submitted more than once; `request.form.getlist` returns every value instead of only one.
key_terms.Client-declared metadata: The filename and content type that accompany an upload; the client supplies them, so they do not prove what the bytes contain.
key_terms.MAX_CONTENT_LENGTH: A Flask setting that caps the accepted request-body size, including multipart overhead; a larger request receives 413 Content Too Large.
key_terms.secure_filename: A Werkzeug helper that removes path separators and unsafe characters from a client filename; it does not validate content and can return an empty string.

worked_examples.title: what secure_filename keeps and removes
worked_examples.interpretation: The client controls the uploaded filename, so the lesson never uses it as a path directly. `secure_filename` stripped the parent-directory segments from both the POSIX and Windows-style names, replaced spaces with underscores, dropped the parentheses and transliterated the accented letters to ASCII. The fourth case is the trap: a name made only of separators becomes an empty string, so a handler that blindly joins it onto an upload directory would write to the directory itself. The lesson guards that with `uploaded.filename or "data.csv"`, and production code should also generate its own storage key. Note that a safe name says nothing about content; the CSV contract check is still required.

title: Cookies, signed sessions and trust
outcome: Inspect a real session cookie, reject tampering and explain why signing does not encrypt its contents.

key_terms.Cookie: A named value a server asks the client to store and send back on later requests that match its domain and path.
key_terms.Signed session cookie: Flask's default session storage, which serializes session data into a cookie and attaches a signature made with the secret key.
key_terms.Tamper detection: Verifying the signature when a cookie returns so that a modified value is rejected and the request starts with an empty session.
key_terms.Signing versus encryption: A signature protects integrity, while encryption protects confidentiality; signed Flask session data remains readable by the client.
key_terms.Cookie attributes: Flags such as Secure, HttpOnly and SameSite that ask browsers to limit transport, script access and cross-site sending, respectively.

worked_examples.title: a signed cookie is readable but not forgeable
worked_examples.interpretation: This uses the same signer configuration Flask's default session interface uses (salt `cookie-session`), so it shows what the lesson's `session` cookie really contains. Anyone holding the cookie decoded `{'visits': 1}` without the secret: signing gives integrity, not confidentiality, so never put a password or private note in it. Replacing the payload with `{"visits":99}` while keeping the old signature raised `BadSignature`, which is why the tampered cookie in the lesson fell back to `visits` 0. If an attacker learned `SECRET_KEY`, they could sign arbitrary values, so the key belongs in configuration, not in source control.

title: WSGI, ASGI and the server boundary
outcome: Compare real synchronous and asynchronous application interfaces without inventing network-performance evidence.

key_terms.WSGI: A synchronous Python interface in which the server passes an environment dictionary and a `start_response` callback, then consumes the response iterable.
key_terms.ASGI: An asynchronous Python interface in which the server passes a connection scope plus awaitable receive and send callables, supporting HTTP and WebSockets.
key_terms.ASGI scope: The dictionary that identifies an interaction's type, such as `http`, and its connection metadata such as method and path.
key_terms.Server boundary: The division between a server such as Uvicorn, which owns network connections, and the application callable, which implements request behavior.
key_terms.Event loop: The asyncio scheduler that runs coroutines and switches between them only at `await` points that yield control.

worked_examples.title: calling WSGI and ASGI applications by hand
code: print([m["type"] for m in messages], messages[1]["body"])
worked_examples.interpretation: Here the server role is played by a few lines of Python. The WSGI application is an ordinary function: the caller passes an `environ` dictionary and a `start_response` callback, and the body comes back as an iterable of bytes when the function returns. The ASGI application is a coroutine that receives a `scope` and two awaitables, then reports its response as a sequence of messages, first the status and headers, then the body. That message stream is what lets ASGI carry WebSockets and long-lived streams that a single WSGI return value cannot express. Flask's test client builds the `environ` for you and FastAPI's client sends these ASGI messages, which is why the lesson can observe `wsgi.version` and `scope["type"]` without any socket. If the ASGI app forgot the `http.response.start` message, a real server would raise an error instead of sending a body.

title: Named routes, redirects and navigation
outcome: Generate URLs from route identities and implement a bounded post-redirect-get flow without open redirects.

key_terms.Endpoint name: The identifier Flask registers for a route, normally the view function's name, used to look up the route instead of hard-coding its path.
key_terms.url_for: Flask's URL builder, which fills path parameters from keyword arguments and places the remaining arguments in the query string.
key_terms.Location header: The response header that names the URL the client should request next after a redirect.
key_terms.303 See Other: A redirect status telling the client to retrieve the Location target with GET, commonly sent after a successful form POST.
key_terms.Post/redirect/get: A pattern in which a state-changing POST answers with a redirect, so a browser refresh repeats a harmless GET instead of the submission.

worked_examples.title: url_for options and redirect statuses
code: from flask import Flask, redirect, url_for
worked_examples.interpretation: `url_for` builds paths from the endpoint name `item`, not from a hand-typed string, so renaming the URL rule later keeps every generated link correct. An unknown keyword such as `sort` became a query parameter, `_anchor` added a fragment, and `_external=True` used the request's scheme and host to produce an absolute URL. All three redirects share the same `Location`; the difference is what the client does next. After a form POST, 303 tells the browser to follow with GET, which is why the lesson uses it, while 307 would repeat the POST with its body. A misspelled endpoint such as `url_for("items")` raises `BuildError` at link-building time instead of producing a broken link.

title: HTTP tests, fixtures and state isolation
outcome: Separate server state, client cookies and factory-scoped fixtures using repeatable request sequences.

key_terms.Application factory: A function such as `make_app()` that builds and returns a new application, with its own state, every time it is called.
key_terms.Fixture: A known starting state, such as a fresh item list, that a test creates explicitly instead of inheriting from earlier code or runs.
key_terms.Cookie jar: The store of cookies a test client keeps and sends on its later requests; each client owns a separate jar.
key_terms.Closure: A function that captures variables from its enclosing scope, which is how the route functions share the factory's item list.
key_terms.State isolation: Arranging tests so each one owns its state and cannot pass or fail because of what another test or client left behind.

worked_examples.title: a module-level list leaks between tests
worked_examples.interpretation: Both calls to `test_create` assert the same story, that creating one item yields a count of 1, but with a module-level list the second run saw 2 because state from the first run survived. The test would pass or fail depending on order, which is the classic flaky-test symptom. Passing a fresh list into each factory call reproduces what the lesson's `make_app` does with its local `items`: every application fixture starts empty. The lesson's `session` counter adds a second boundary, since two clients of one application share server state but not cookies. In pytest, a fixture that calls the factory gives every test its own application; scoping that fixture to `module` would reintroduce the leak.

title: Resource-oriented API design and REST constraints
outcome: Design consistent resource identities and state transitions, explaining statelessness and representation tradeoffs.

key_terms.Resource: An identifiable thing an API exposes, such as one task, addressed by its own URL.
key_terms.Representation: The data an API chooses to expose about a resource, here an ID and a title, which need not mirror every internal field.
key_terms.Self link: A URL in a response that identifies the returned resource, generated from the registered read route so a client can follow it.
key_terms.Collection endpoint: A path such as `/tasks` where POST creates a new member with a server-allocated ID, so repeating the POST creates another resource.
key_terms.REST constraints: The architectural properties of client/server separation, stateless interactions, cacheability, a uniform interface and layering, which JSON routes do not satisfy automatically.

worked_examples.title: Location headers and a collection resource
code: from flask import Flask, request, url_for
worked_examples.interpretation: The POST targeted the collection `/tasks` and the server, not the client, chose identifier 1. The 201 response advertised the new member's URL in the standard `Location` header, and the client followed that header instead of building `/tasks/1` itself. The lesson puts the same link in a `links.self` body field; both forms let the server change its URL layout without breaking clients. The collection and the member are separate resources with separate representations, which is the core of resource-oriented design. Using `len(tasks) + 1` is only safe in this single-threaded fixture: after a deletion it would reuse an identifier, which is why the lesson keeps a monotonic `count(1)` instead.

title: Flask application factories and configuration
outcome: Construct isolated Flask applications with explicit test and deployment settings.

key_terms.Application factory: A function that constructs and configures a new Flask application on each call, giving tests and deployments a deliberate initialization boundary.
key_terms.app.config: The application's configuration mapping; `from_mapping` establishes defaults and `update` applies explicit overrides.
key_terms.Explicit boolean parsing: Converting configuration text into True or False with defined rules; `bool("false")` is True because every nonempty string is truthy.
key_terms.Instance isolation: Each application object owning its own mutable state, such as a counter in `app.extensions`, so two applications never share request counts.
key_terms.Configuration allowlist: An explicit list of harmless settings an endpoint may return, which keeps signing keys and credentials out of responses.

worked_examples.title: parsing environment overrides into typed configuration
worked_examples.interpretation: Environment variables are always strings. `from_prefixed_env` strips the `DEMO_` prefix and tries to parse each value as JSON, so `"5"` became the integer 5 and `"false"` became the boolean False, while `west` was not valid JSON and stayed a string. The last line repeats the trap that the lesson's `enabled` helper exists to prevent: `bool("false")` is True because any nonempty string is truthy. The factory layers its sources in a fixed order, defaults, then environment, then the test mapping, so the test application saw True without changing the production object. Both applications were built from one function and share no configuration dictionary, which is what lets a test suite create many isolated instances. A typo such as `DEMO_FEATURE_ENABLE` would add an unused key, not an error, so validate the settings your factory requires.

title: Flask blueprints and error boundaries
outcome: Compose routes through blueprints and distinguish application-wide from blueprint error handling.

key_terms.Blueprint: A named group of Flask routes and handlers that an application registers, optionally under a URL prefix such as `/api`.
key_terms.Qualified endpoint: A blueprint route's endpoint name, such as `api.item`, which identifies the route for URL building and differs from its path.
key_terms.abort: A Flask function that ends handling by raising an HTTP exception for a given status code, such as 404.
key_terms.Blueprint error handler: A handler registered on a blueprint that formats errors raised while one of that blueprint's routes is handling a request.
key_terms.Application error handler: A handler registered on the application itself, needed for errors such as an unmatched URL that occur before any blueprint owns the request.

worked_examples.title: one blueprint registered under two prefixes
code: from flask import Blueprint, Flask, url_for
print(sorted(r.endpoint for r in app.url_map.iter_rules() if r.endpoint != "static"))
worked_examples.interpretation: A blueprint is a recorded set of routes and handlers, not an application, so registering it twice created two real URL rules. The second registration needed a distinct `name`, otherwise Flask refuses the duplicate, and that name became the endpoint prefix: `api_v2.item` builds `/v2/items/3`. The 405 handler was attached with `app_errorhandler`, which installs it on the whole application, unlike the lesson's `api.errorhandler(404)` that only applies to errors raised inside the blueprint's own views. That difference matters because a 405 or an unmatched URL is decided by the router before any blueprint view runs; a blueprint-local 405 handler would never fire. Printing `app.url_map` is the quickest way to confirm what a registration actually produced.

title: Flask request context, application context and cleanup
outcome: Use request-local state and teardown correctly, including an exception path.

key_terms.Application context: The Flask context that makes `current_app` and `g` available; it can be pushed without any request.
key_terms.Request context: The Flask context pushed for one request, which makes `request` and `session` available to code running during that request.
key_terms.g object: A namespace that belongs to the application context and commonly holds a resource for the duration of one request.
key_terms.Teardown hook: A function registered with `teardown_request` that runs after each request, successful or failed, and receives any exception so it can release resources.
key_terms.Context-local proxy: An object such as `request` or `current_app` that refers to the value of the currently active context instead of a fixed module global.

worked_examples.title: the order of request hooks on success and failure
worked_examples.interpretation: Unlike the lesson, this application leaves `TESTING` off, so the unhandled `KeyError` was converted into a 500 response instead of propagating into the test. The hooks ran in the same order both times: `before_request`, then `after_request` on the response that was actually sent, then `teardown_request`. Only teardown received the original exception, which is why the lesson closes its resource there: `after_request` sees a 500 response object but not the `KeyError`, and it is skipped entirely when an exception escapes in testing mode. With `TESTING=True` the second request would raise `KeyError` in the caller and the log would end at teardown. Each request got its own `g`, so the connection stored on the first request was not visible on the second.

title: Flask and SQLAlchemy transaction ownership
outcome: Scope a real database session to a request and verify successful commit and failed-operation rollback.

key_terms.Transaction: A group of database changes that commit together or roll back together, so a batch never partially succeeds.
key_terms.ORM session: The SQLAlchemy object that tracks Python objects and issues their SQL; this example creates one per operation from a session factory.
key_terms.Session.begin(): A SQLAlchemy context manager that commits when its block exits normally and rolls back when an exception escapes.
key_terms.Flush: Sending pending changes to the database inside the current transaction without committing them, which can surface a constraint failure early.
key_terms.IntegrityError: The SQLAlchemy exception raised when a statement violates a database constraint, translated here into a 409 Conflict response.

worked_examples.title: one transaction versus a commit per row
code: from sqlalchemy import String, create_engine, select
from sqlalchemy.orm import DeclarativeBase, Mapped, Session, mapped_column
worked_examples.interpretation: Both runs submitted the same batch, `temporary` followed by the duplicate `existing`, and both hit the unique constraint. Committing each row separately left `temporary` behind, a half-applied request that the client was told had failed. Wrapping the whole batch in one `db.begin()` block made the failure roll back everything, so the table returned to its prior single row. That is the ownership rule the lesson's `/batch` view follows: one HTTP request owns one transaction, and the handler translates `IntegrityError` into 409 only after the rollback has happened. Reordering the batch to put `existing` first would make the per-row version fail before inserting anything, which is why a passing test with one ordering does not prove the per-row design is safe.

title: Flask relational queries and deterministic pagination
outcome: Avoid accidental unordered pagination and inspect bounded relationship loading.

key_terms.Deterministic ordering: An ORDER BY on a unique key, such as item ID, so every request sees the rows in the same sequence.
key_terms.Keyset pagination: Fetching the next page with a condition such as `Item.id > after`, where the last observed ordering key serves as the cursor.
key_terms.Offset pagination: Skipping a counted number of rows in the ordered result, which can skip or repeat rows when earlier data changes between requests.
key_terms.Explicit join: A single query that combines items with their owners and selects only the needed columns, avoiding one extra owner query per item.
key_terms.Tie-breaker: A unique column appended to a nonunique sort key, such as a timestamp, so the ordering and any cursor built from it are unambiguous.

worked_examples.title: a tie-breaker makes keyset pages deterministic
code: db.execute(text("CREATE TABLE items (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, score INTEGER)"))
"SELECT score, id FROM items WHERE (score, id) > (:s, :i) "
worked_examples.interpretation: Sorting only by `score` would leave the order of rows 1 and 3, and of 2 and 4, undefined, so a database could return them differently between requests and a cursor of `score > 50` would skip row 3 entirely. Adding `id` as a unique tie-breaker gives a total order, and the row-value comparison `(score, id) > (:s, :i)` resumes exactly after the last row the client saw. The three pages cover all five rows once with no duplicates. The lesson's simpler cursor uses `Item.id` alone because its order is already the primary key. If a new item with score 60 were inserted between page requests, it would appear on the second page without shifting any other row, which offset pagination cannot promise.

title: Flask forms and CSRF protection
outcome: Use actual Flask-WTF validation and CSRF behavior instead of treating a signed cookie as sufficient protection.

key_terms.CSRF: Cross-site request forgery: another site causes a browser to send a state-changing request that carries the user's ambient credentials.
key_terms.Ambient credentials: Credentials such as cookies that a browser attaches automatically to matching requests regardless of which page initiated them.
key_terms.CSRF token: A session-bound secret rendered into the form and required on submission, which a forging site cannot read; Flask-WTF rejects a missing token with 400.
key_terms.hidden_tag(): A Flask-WTF form method that renders the form's hidden fields, including the CSRF token.
key_terms.Field validator: A rule such as DataRequired or Length that checks a submitted value, independently of CSRF validation.

worked_examples.title: a CSRF token is bound to one session
code: if "csrf_raw" not in session or not submitted:
worked_examples.interpretation: This is a simplified model of what Flask-WTF does behind `form.hidden_tag()`: a random value lives in the signed session cookie and the page embeds a keyed digest of it. The victim's own form submission passed. An attacker can load the site and obtain a perfectly valid token, but it is valid only for the attacker's session, so replaying it against the victim's session failed. A missing token and a session with no stored value were both rejected, matching the lesson's 400 for a POST without `csrf_token`. `hmac.compare_digest` avoids leaking how many leading characters matched through timing. The real extension also adds an expiry timestamp, so an old token copied from a cached page would eventually be refused even within the same session.

title: Flask login, logout and session behavior
outcome: Use Flask-Login with a real client cookie jar and distinguish authenticated and anonymous requests.

key_terms.Authentication: Establishing a caller's identity from credentials such as a username and password.
key_terms.User loader: The Flask-Login callback that maps the user ID stored in the session back to a user object on each request.
key_terms.login_user: The Flask-Login function that records an authenticated identity in the session; `logout_user` removes it.
key_terms.login_required: A Flask-Login decorator that refuses anonymous callers; this example's unauthorized handler answers with JSON 401 instead of a login-page redirect.
key_terms.Password hash: A salted one-way transformation of a password, created with `generate_password_hash` and checked with `check_password_hash` so plaintext is never stored.

worked_examples.title: what a stored password hash contains
worked_examples.interpretation: The stored value starts with its own recipe: the scrypt algorithm and its cost parameters, followed by a 16-character random salt and the derived key. Hashing the same password twice produced different strings because each call chose a new salt, so you can never verify a login by hashing the input and comparing strings with `==`; `check_password_hash` reads the method and salt from the stored value and repeats the derivation. One changed capital letter and one trailing space both failed, which is why the lesson's login view should not silently strip or lowercase passwords. Because the parameters travel with each hash, raising the cost later only affects newly stored passwords, and existing users still verify.

title: Flask authorization and object ownership
outcome: Apply object-level ownership checks and prevent list endpoints from exposing another user's data.

key_terms.Authorization: Deciding what an authenticated caller may see or change, separately from establishing who the caller is.
key_terms.Object-level authorization: Checking a requested record's owner against the trusted current user before returning it, even when IDs are hard to guess.
key_terms.Ownership scoping: Filtering list queries by `current_user.id` so a caller receives only its own records.
key_terms.Nondisclosing 404: Returning the same 404 response for an absent record and for one owned by someone else, so the response does not reveal that it exists.

worked_examples.title: 403 versus 404 for someone else's record
worked_examples.interpretation: Alice probed three identifiers: her own record 1, Bob's record 2 and the missing record 3. With the 403 policy the statuses for 2 and 3 differed, so Alice learned that record 2 exists even though she cannot read it; enumerating identifiers would map out every other customer's records. Returning 404 for both made the foreign and the absent record indistinguishable, which is the lesson's rule. The `X-Fixture-User` header stands in for `current_user` only to keep the example small: a real request header is client-controlled and must never decide identity, in the same way the lesson ignores `?owner=bob`. A 403 is still reasonable when existence is already public, such as a shared document whose title is visible.

title: Flask uploads, downloads and path boundaries
outcome: Validate uploaded content and safely select owned download files without trusting submitted filenames.

key_terms.Path traversal: An attack that uses segments such as `..` or symbolic links to reach files outside the intended directory.
key_terms.Canonical path: An absolute path with symbolic links and `..` segments resolved, obtained here with `Path.resolve()`.
key_terms.Storage root: The owned directory that every served file must stay inside; it must itself be resolved before candidates are compared with it.
key_terms.send_file: Flask's helper for sending a file's bytes as a response, called only after the resolved path passes the boundary check.
key_terms.Time-of-check/time-of-use: A race in which the filesystem changes between validating a path and opening it, so the checked file is not the served file.

worked_examples.title: why a string prefix check is not a path boundary
worked_examples.interpretation: The second row shows the classic bug: `/srv/uploads_old` begins with the characters `/srv/uploads`, so a `startswith` check accepts a sibling directory. `is_relative_to` compares whole path components and correctly rejects it. The third row shows the limit of pure path objects: they do not interpret `..`, so even `is_relative_to` says the unresolved path is inside the root. That is why the lesson calls `resolve(strict=True)` first, which collapses `..`, follows symbolic links such as `linked.txt` and requires the file to exist, and only then checks containment. Checking before resolving, or resolving without the containment check, each leaves one of the lesson's two 404 cases open.

title: Flask conditional requests and cache policy
outcome: Implement ETag comparisons and choose public, private and non-cacheable response policies deliberately.

key_terms.ETag: A validator string that identifies one specific version of a representation, here a hash of the fixed JSON bytes.
key_terms.If-None-Match: A request header carrying an ETag the client already holds, asking the server to send the body only if the representation has changed.
key_terms.304 Not Modified: A response without a body telling the client that its stored representation is still current.
key_terms.Cache-Control: The header that states reuse policy, such as `public, max-age=60` for shared caching or `private, no-store` for an account response.
key_terms.Strong validator: An ETag that changes whenever the representation's bytes change, so a match means the stored bytes are identical.

worked_examples.title: Last-Modified as a second validator
code: from flask import Flask, Response, request
worked_examples.interpretation: The server sent a timestamp validator instead of the lesson's ETag. A client that echoed the same date in `If-Modified-Since` got 304 with an empty body, while a client whose copy dated from February received the full 16 bytes. The `max-age=0, must-revalidate` policy says the response may be stored but must be checked on every use, so the savings come from small 304 responses rather than from skipping requests, unlike the lesson's `max-age=60` resource. Timestamps have one-second resolution: two edits within the same second would share a Last-Modified value and a client could keep the stale copy, which is why an ETag derived from the exact bytes is the stronger validator when both are available.

title: Flask CLI and versioned schema changes
outcome: Exercise application CLI commands and a bounded migration lifecycle with actual database effects.

key_terms.Flask CLI command: A Click function registered on the application for an operational task such as initialization and invoked by name instead of through HTTP.
key_terms.CLI runner: Flask's testing helper that invokes a registered command in process and captures its exit code and output.
key_terms.Schema migration: A controlled change to an existing database schema that preserves existing data, such as adding a column.
key_terms.Server default: A column default applied by the database, which lets existing rows receive a value when a nonnullable column is added.
key_terms.Revision history: The ordered Alembic revision files and version table that record which migrations a database has applied.

worked_examples.title: CLI options, exit codes and failure output
code: raise click.ClickException(f"refusing to downgrade from {current} to {target}")
output: 1 Error: refusing to downgrade from 2 to 1
worked_examples.interpretation: The test runner invoked the registered command in process and captured both the exit code and the text an operator would see. The second run was a safe no-op, the same rerun property the lesson checks with `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS`. Raising `ClickException` turned the refused downgrade into exit code 1 with a readable message rather than a traceback, and Click itself returned exit code 2 for the missing required option before the function body ran. Deployment scripts rely on those nonzero codes to stop a rollout, so a command that printed an error but exited 0 would let a failed migration go unnoticed. The final list shows revisions 1 and 2 were applied exactly once despite four invocations.

title: Flask outbound clients, timeouts and error translation
outcome: Use a deterministic HTTP mock transport and translate upstream failures without claiming a live service test.

key_terms.Upstream service: Another service that a handler calls while building its own response, adding latency, failures and a second response contract.
key_terms.Read timeout: A limit on how long the client waits for response data before raising a timeout exception instead of hanging.
key_terms.MockTransport: An HTTPX2 transport that answers requests by calling a Python handler instead of performing network I/O.
key_terms.Error translation: Mapping upstream failures to distinct local responses, here 504 Gateway Timeout for a timeout and 502 Bad Gateway for an upstream error.

worked_examples.title: separate connect and read timeouts
worked_examples.interpretation: `Timeout(5.0, connect=1.0)` keeps the 5 second default for reading, writing and waiting for a pooled connection but fails fast when the upstream host does not accept a connection within 1 second. Both timeout classes share the `TimeoutException` base, so the lesson's single `except` maps them to 504, yet they mean different things: a connect timeout means the request never reached the upstream and is safe to retry, while a read timeout may follow a request the upstream already processed. The 429 response did not raise until `raise_for_status`, and its `Retry-After` value of 3 is information the lesson's generic 502 discards. A proxy that should honor backpressure could return 503 with that header instead.

title: Flask async views and background-work limits
outcome: Explain what async changes under WSGI and distinguish request-scoped work from durable jobs.

key_terms.Async view: A Flask view defined with `async def`, which the WSGI async bridge runs to completion on an event loop created for that request.
key_terms.asyncio.gather: A function that awaits several awaitables concurrently and returns all their results, so the response can depend on every one of them.
key_terms.asyncio.create_task: A function that schedules a coroutine to run on its own; under Flask's WSGI bridge a task still pending when the view returns is cancelled.
key_terms.Durable job: Work recorded in persistent storage and executed by a separate worker, so it survives the request, process restarts and failures.

worked_examples.title: an orphaned task versus an awaited task
worked_examples.interpretation: Each `asyncio.run` call here stands in for one Flask request: Flask hands an async view to a fresh event loop through `asgiref`, and that loop is closed once the view returns. Both views report success, yet only the owned task ever printed `finished`. When the first loop shut down, `asyncio.run` cancelled every task still pending, so the orphan ran its `finally` block and vanished halfway through its work. Nothing in the response warns you, which is why the lesson's `/spawned` route returns 200 while its event list proves the background job was cancelled. The rule that follows is narrow: inside a Flask async view, only work you await before returning is guaranteed to run. Email sending, report building and anything that must survive the request belong in a durable queue with its own worker process, not in `create_task`.

title: Flask application walkthrough
outcome: Integrate routing, forms, persistence and authorization in a complete finite client investigation and an owned application project.

key_terms.Session reset at login: Clearing existing session data before recording the authenticated user, which also invalidates the earlier CSRF token so the client must fetch a fresh one.
key_terms.Parameterized query: SQL in which values such as owner and title are passed separately as `?` parameters, so the database treats them as data and never as SQL syntax.
key_terms.Server-assigned ownership: Setting a record's owner from the authenticated session instead of from any field the client supplies.
key_terms.Connection context manager: Using `with sqlite3.connect(path) as db` so a successful block commits and an exception rolls back; the context does not close the connection itself.

worked_examples.title: why login starts by clearing the session
worked_examples.interpretation: Picture one browser on a shared desk. Bob signs in as an administrator and walks away without logging out, then Alice signs in. When the login route only overwrites `user`, every other key from Bob's session rides along, and Alice silently inherits `role: admin`. The integrated program's `login` view calls `session.clear()` before writing `user` for exactly this reason: authentication is a boundary, and nothing written before it should be trusted after it. The same habit protects any flag you later add to the session, such as a cart, a pending redirect or a cached permission.

title: FastAPI typed paths, queries and response contracts
outcome: Build typed routes with actual validation and response behavior, linking annotations to generated API metadata.

key_terms.Path parameter: A typed function argument named in the route path, such as `item_id`, that FastAPI converts and validates before the handler runs.
key_terms.Query parameter: A function argument that is not part of the path, read from the query string to modify the requested representation, such as `limit`.
key_terms.Annotated: The `typing.Annotated` form that pairs a Python type with FastAPI metadata such as `Path(ge=1)`, from which the framework builds validation.
key_terms.response_model: The declared output schema FastAPI uses to validate and serialize the returned value and to document the response.
key_terms.OpenAPI: The machine-readable API description FastAPI generates from route declarations, including parameters, constraints and response schemas.

worked_examples.title: path and query constraints as one pydantic model
code: from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, ValidationError
print("422", [(e["loc"][0], e["type"]) for e in error.errors()])
worked_examples.interpretation: Path segments and query strings arrive as text, so the inputs here are strings on purpose. Pydantic's default lax mode turns `"7"` into the integer 7, fills the missing `limit` with its default of 2 and rejects `"seven"` before any bounds are checked. The last input breaks two rules at once and pydantic reports both, which is why a FastAPI 422 body lists every failing parameter instead of stopping at the first. `Path(ge=1)` and `Query(ge=1, le=5)` in the lesson's route compile down to these same constraints, so the error types you see here are the ones a client of `/items/{item_id}` receives.

title: Pydantic models, strictness and serialization
outcome: Separate input models, output models and internal state while inspecting validation and serialization differences.

key_terms.BaseModel: The Pydantic base class whose subclasses declare typed fields and validate incoming data into model instances.
key_terms.PATCH: An HTTP method for a partial update that should change only the fields the request actually supplies.
key_terms.Fields set: Pydantic's record of which fields the caller supplied, kept separately from values that came from defaults.
key_terms.exclude_unset: A `model_dump` option that omits fields the caller did not supply, so an empty PATCH produces an empty update mapping.
key_terms.Explicit null: A field sent with the value `null`, which is a deliberate instruction to clear an optional value rather than an omission.

worked_examples.title: applying three PATCH bodies to one record
code: from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict, Field, ValidationError
age: Annotated[int, Field(strict=True, ge=0)] | None = None
worked_examples.interpretation: The `naive` lines show what happens when a handler merges the full dump: a body that only mentioned `age` wiped `display_name`, and a body that only cleared the name also erased the age. Dumping with `exclude_unset=True` keeps exactly the fields the client sent, including an explicit `null`, so the `kept` record changes one field per request. Strict mode refuses `True` for `age` even though Python treats booleans as integers, and `extra="forbid"` stops a client from smuggling a `role` field into the update.

title: FastAPI dependency injection and overrides
outcome: Scope dependencies, compose authorization/data services and replace them deliberately in tests.

key_terms.Dependency: A callable that FastAPI resolves for a request and injects into the route, after first resolving that callable's own dependencies.
key_terms.Depends: The FastAPI marker, usually written inside `Annotated`, declaring that a parameter's value comes from a dependency callable.
key_terms.Yield dependency: A generator dependency in which code before `yield` acquires a resource and code after it performs cleanup, even when the route raises.
key_terms.Dependency override: An entry in `app.dependency_overrides` that replaces one dependency for a test; it must be removed afterward so later tests use the real dependency.
key_terms.Request scope: The lifetime of one request, appropriate for a database session, in contrast to the application lifespan suited to a shared client pool.

worked_examples.title: how a yield dependency sees a handler failure
worked_examples.interpretation: This is a plain Python model of what FastAPI does with a `yield` dependency: run the code before `yield`, hand the value to the endpoint, then resume the generator when the request ends. When the endpoint raises, the exception is thrown back in at the `yield`, so the dependency can roll back before `finally` closes the resource. The third call swaps in a fake provider, the job `app.dependency_overrides` does in the lesson, and the event list proves the real repository never opened. Notice that `rollback` appears once: a successful read reached `close` without passing through the `except` branch.

title: FastAPI lifespan and resource ownership
outcome: Initialize and close shared resources through actual lifespan events, including failed-request cleanup.

key_terms.Lifespan: An async context manager given to FastAPI that performs setup before the application serves requests and cleanup at shutdown.
key_terms.app.state: An attribute namespace on the application where lifespan setup stores prepared resources for routes to use.
key_terms.TestClient context: Entering `with TestClient(app)` so that lifespan startup and shutdown actually run around the test's requests.
key_terms.Process-local state: Data owned by one server process; four workers create four lifespans and therefore four separate copies.
key_terms.Readiness: A service's ability to perform work that needs its dependencies, which is a stronger claim than the process merely being alive.

worked_examples.title: lifespan state delivered on every request
worked_examples.interpretation: FastAPI is built on Starlette, and this snippet uses Starlette directly to show a second way to share a lifespan resource. The lesson's program stores its resource on `app.state`; here the lifespan yields a dictionary instead, and Starlette copies it onto `request.state` for every request. Either way the resource is created once at startup, not per request. The two `log` prints show the boundary: inside the `with TestClient(app)` block only startup has run, and shutdown fires when the block exits. Creating the client without `with` would skip the lifespan entirely, which is the `AttributeError` the lesson deliberately provokes.

title: Async Python, blocking work and cancellation
outcome: Measure cooperative concurrency with explicit synchronization rather than unqualified timing claims.

key_terms.Coroutine: The object an `async def` function returns; its body runs only when it is awaited or scheduled as a task.
key_terms.Suspension point: An `await` on an operation that yields control, where the event loop may switch to another ready task.
key_terms.Blocking call: A synchronous operation, such as file or HTTP I/O or a long CPU loop, that holds the event-loop thread and stops other tasks from progressing.
key_terms.Concurrency versus parallelism: Concurrency means several tasks are in progress at once; parallelism means instructions execute simultaneously, which one event-loop thread does not provide.
key_terms.Cancellation: Delivering `CancelledError` to a task at its next await; the caller should await the cancelled task so its `finally` cleanup can finish.

worked_examples.title: a blocking call starves the event loop
worked_examples.interpretation: The ticker stands in for every other request an async server is handling. With `time.sleep` inside an `async def`, the handler never reaches an `await`, so the ticker cannot take a single step until the sleep ends. Moving the same blocking call into `asyncio.to_thread` gives the loop a suspension point, and all three ticks run while the thread waits. In FastAPI this is why a blocking database driver or `requests.get` inside an `async def` endpoint stalls unrelated clients, while a plain `def` endpoint is run in a threadpool for you.

title: FastAPI asynchronous database sessions
outcome: Use real SQLAlchemy async sessions with bounded SQLite fixtures and correct event-loop ownership.

key_terms.Async engine: The SQLAlchemy object that manages database connectivity and pooling for asyncio code; one engine is normally shared by the application.
key_terms.AsyncSession: An asyncio SQLAlchemy session that tracks one unit of work and its transaction; each request borrows its own instead of sharing one.
key_terms.async_sessionmaker: A factory bound to the engine that creates a new AsyncSession for each request.
key_terms.aiosqlite: An asyncio driver for SQLite that lets the fixture run real SQL offline, although its locking behavior differs from PostgreSQL.
key_terms.Rollback after failure: Ending the failed transaction once the database rejects a write, which is required before the session can be used again.

worked_examples.title: what expire_on_commit costs after a commit
code: from sqlalchemy import String, create_engine, event
from sqlalchemy.orm import DeclarativeBase, Mapped, Session, mapped_column
def record(conn, cursor, sql, params, context, many):
worked_examples.interpretation: This synchronous session makes a hidden query visible. With the default `expire_on_commit=True`, every attribute is marked stale at commit, so simply reading `item.name` afterwards issued a fresh `SELECT`. A synchronous session can do that quietly, but an `AsyncSession` cannot perform implicit I/O on attribute access and raises `MissingGreenlet` instead. That is why the lesson's `async_sessionmaker` passes `expire_on_commit=False`: objects returned from an async endpoint after commit must already hold their values.

title: Transactions, optimistic concurrency and idempotency keys
outcome: Protect updates and repeated requests with explicit version and request-identity contracts.

key_terms.Optimistic concurrency: Letting clients read freely but applying an update only if the resource's version still matches the version the client observed.
key_terms.If-Match: A precondition header carrying the observed version; this service returns 428 when it is missing and 412 Precondition Failed when it is stale.
key_terms.Conditional update: A single SQL UPDATE whose WHERE clause checks the version, so the database evaluates the check and the write together.
key_terms.Idempotency key: A client-chosen identifier for one logical command, stored with the input and outcome so a retry returns the original result.
key_terms.409 Conflict: The response here when an idempotency key is reused with different input, which is refused instead of running a new command.

worked_examples.title: two writers holding the same ETag
code: db.execute("CREATE TABLE items(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, title TEXT, version INTEGER)")
"UPDATE items SET title=?, version=version+1 WHERE id=1 AND version=?",
print(etag, patch("from alice", etag), patch("from bob", etag))
worked_examples.interpretation: Alice and Bob both read the item while it was at version 1 and both sent that validator back in `If-Match`. The version test lives inside the `UPDATE` itself, so the check and the write happen atomically: Alice's statement matched one row and bumped the version, and Bob's identical statement matched zero rows. Reading the version in Python and then updating in a second statement would leave a window where both writers pass the check, and Bob would silently overwrite Alice.

title: FastAPI response filtering and sensitive fields
outcome: Verify that internal fields do not leak through serialization and explain when response validation fails.

key_terms.Response model: The declared public representation FastAPI uses to filter and validate whatever object a route returns.
key_terms.Output filtering: Leaving fields outside the response model, such as an owner key or password hash, out of the serialized response.
key_terms.Response validation: Checking returned data against the response model; a failure is a server defect and produces 500, not a client error.
key_terms.Data leakage: Exposure of sensitive values through any path, including debug logs and exception messages that never pass through the response model.

worked_examples.title: a response model as an allow list
code: from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict, ValidationError
worked_examples.interpretation: A `response_model` works as an allow list, and these three calls show the pieces FastAPI relies on. The first input is an ordinary object shaped like an ORM row; `from_attributes=True` lets the model read its attributes, and `password_hash` is dropped because the model never declared it. The second input is a dictionary with an extra `internal_role` key, which the default `extra="ignore"` setting discards while the string `"2"` is coerced to an integer. The third input is the server's own mistake, so validation fails on both fields. In the lesson's `/broken` route FastAPI turns that failure into `ResponseValidationError`, which a test sees as an exception and a client sees only as a bare 500. Keeping the public model separate from the storage model is what makes the filtering automatic: adding a sensitive column to the row later cannot leak unless someone also adds it to `PublicUser`.

title: FastAPI errors and problem-details documents
outcome: Implement predictable application errors and preserve safe distinction between validation and server failures.

key_terms.Problem details: A JSON error representation with type, title, status and instance fields, sent with the media type `application/problem+json`.
key_terms.Problem type: A stable identifier, here a URN, that names a class of problem so clients can branch on it instead of on message wording.
key_terms.Exception handler: A function registered with `app.exception_handler` that converts one exception class into a controlled HTTP response.
key_terms.RequestValidationError: The FastAPI exception raised for invalid input, mapped here to 422 with safe field locations.
key_terms.Unexpected defect: An unhandled internal exception, answered with a generic 500 while detailed diagnostics stay in controlled internal logs.

worked_examples.title: problem details from Starlette exception handlers
worked_examples.interpretation: FastAPI's `exception_handler` decorator registers handlers on the Starlette layer shown here. The third path is the instructive one: no route raised anything, yet the router's own 404 also came back as problem JSON, because the router raises the same `HTTPException` class that the handler catches. The `ZeroDivisionError` text never reaches the client; the catch-all handler replaced it with a generic title while the full traceback stays available to server logs.

title: Bearer tokens, JWT claims and authentication
outcome: Validate signatures and intended issuer/audience/expiry with real token libraries and explicit failure cases.

key_terms.Bearer token: A credential that grants access to whoever presents it, sent in the `Authorization: Bearer` header.
key_terms.JWT: A JSON Web Token: a compact signed set of claims whose decoded JSON proves nothing until the signature and claims are verified.
key_terms.Signature verification: Checking a token with the issuer's public key and an explicit allowed algorithm list, here only RS256, instead of trusting the token header.
key_terms.Issuer and audience: The `iss` claim names the expected issuing authority and `aud` names the intended recipient; a valid token for another API is refused.
key_terms.Expiration claim: The `exp` claim, after which the recipient must reject the token even though its signature remains valid.

worked_examples.title: what jwt.decode refuses and why
code: from datetime import UTC, datetime, timedelta
output: InvalidAlgorithmError The specified alg value is not allowed
worked_examples.interpretation: This uses a shared HMAC secret to keep the snippet short, while the lesson signs with an RSA key pair so the API only needs the public half. The unsigned token names `alg: none` in its own header, and a verifier that trusted that header would accept it with no signature at all. Passing `algorithms=["HS256"]` pins the accepted algorithm on the server side, so PyJWT refuses the token before looking at any claim. The second failure carries a valid signature but was minted for a different API, and the audience check stops it from being replayed against this one.

title: Cookies, CSRF, CORS and browser origins
outcome: Distinguish authentication, cross-origin permissions and CSRF protections with actual middleware/client observations.

key_terms.SameSite: A cookie attribute, here `lax`, that limits when a browser attaches the cookie to requests initiated from another site.
key_terms.CSRF token: An unpredictable value bound to the session that a state-changing request must echo, which a cross-site page cannot read or guess.
key_terms.Constant-time comparison: Comparing secrets with `hmac.compare_digest` so the comparison time does not reveal how many leading characters matched.
key_terms.CORS: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing: browser rules about which other origins may read responses, which do not stop a request from being sent.
key_terms.Preflight request: An OPTIONS request a browser sends before certain cross-origin requests to ask whether the method and headers are allowed.

worked_examples.title: CORS decides what the browser reads, not what the server runs
worked_examples.interpretation: The preflight for the foreign origin was refused with 400, yet the direct POST from that origin still reached the handler, and `calls` records both. The only thing CORS withheld was the `access-control-allow-origin` header, which tells a browser not to let the calling page read the response. A form post or a script that skips the preflight can still cause the side effect. That is why the lesson's `/change` route checks `Origin` and compares the `X-CSRF-Token` header itself instead of trusting the middleware to block writes.

title: API scopes, roles and tenant boundaries
outcome: Enforce both action-level permission and object ownership rather than relying on token presence alone.

key_terms.Authorization: Deciding what an identified caller may do to a particular resource, which is separate from authenticating who the caller is.
key_terms.Scope: A permission for a class of operation, such as writing notes, carried by a credential and checked by the endpoint.
key_terms.SecurityScopes: The FastAPI object that passes the scopes an endpoint requires into the dependency that checks the credential.
key_terms.Tenant boundary: The separation of one customer or workspace's data from another's, enforced in the lookup even for a caller with the right scope.
key_terms.Ownership predicate: A query condition that limits results to objects the caller owns, so an object outside that scope behaves as missing.

worked_examples.title: checking scopes as a set, not as a substring
worked_examples.interpretation: An OAuth access token usually carries its scopes as one space separated string. Testing `required in granted_claim` searches characters, so `notes:write` matched inside `notes:write-drafts` and a draft-only token would pass a full write check. Splitting the claim into tokens and comparing sets fixes it, which is exactly what the lesson's `authorize` dependency does with `issubset`. Even a correct scope check only says what kind of action the token may attempt; the ownership and tenant comparison inside `update` still decides which note it may touch.

title: FastAPI file handling and streaming responses
outcome: Bound uploaded data and construct finite streamed responses while retaining content and cleanup contracts.

key_terms.UploadFile: FastAPI's file-like wrapper for a multipart upload whose contents may be spooled to temporary storage rather than held in memory.
key_terms.Bounded read: Reading at most one byte past the allowed size so an oversized upload is detected, here with 413, without reading the whole body.
key_terms.FileResponse: A response that streams a server-chosen file and supplies its metadata and byte-range handling.
key_terms.Range request: A request for part of a resource, answered with 206 Partial Content, or 416 when the requested range cannot be satisfied.
key_terms.StreamingResponse: A response whose body is produced chunk by chunk from an iterator, here a finite sequence of CSV lines.

worked_examples.title: three Range headers against one small file
worked_examples.interpretation: The file is 11 bytes long, and each `Content-Range` header names the inclusive byte positions returned plus that total. An open ended range such as `bytes=6-` runs to the last byte, while `bytes=-3` is a suffix range meaning the final three bytes, not positions zero to three. Download managers and video players resume with these forms, so a hand-written range parser that only handles `start-end` breaks them. `FileResponse` in FastAPI inherits this parsing from Starlette, and the lesson's 416 case covers a start position past the end of the file.

title: Background tasks, queues and durable work
outcome: Compare request-attached tasks with an explicit durable-job design and label eager-task evidence honestly.

key_terms.202 Accepted: A status meaning the request was accepted for processing under the application's contract, not that the work has completed.
key_terms.BackgroundTasks: A FastAPI mechanism that runs a callback after the response in the same serving process, so the work is lost if that process dies.
key_terms.Eager mode: A Celery test setting, `task_always_eager`, that runs a task locally and immediately instead of sending it through a broker.
key_terms.Message broker: The service that holds queued task messages for workers; an in-memory broker is process-local and does not persist them.
key_terms.Job ledger: Persistent records of operations and their states that a separate worker can claim, retry and reconcile.

worked_examples.title: a failing background task silently drops the rest
worked_examples.interpretation: FastAPI's `BackgroundTasks` is this Starlette class, so the behavior carries over directly. The client received 202 Accepted, the status that promises the work will happen, but the tasks ran one after another in the same process after the response, and the exception in the second task stopped the third. Grace never got her message, and nothing in the HTTP exchange could report that, because the response had already been sent. A server restart between the response and the tasks would lose all three in the same quiet way. This is the gap the lesson points at when it contrasts in-process tasks with a Celery queue: a broker keeps each job as its own record, a worker retries a job that failed, and one failure does not cancel unrelated jobs. Use `BackgroundTasks` only for work you can afford to lose, such as warming a cache.

title: WebSocket messages, validation and close behavior
outcome: Exercise a finite real ASGI WebSocket exchange and explain connection/authentication/resource boundaries.

key_terms.WebSocket handshake: The initial HTTP exchange that the server accepts or refuses before any messages flow over the long-lived connection.
key_terms.Origin check: Comparing the handshake's Origin header with an expected value, which blocks unwanted browser initiation but is not authentication.
key_terms.Message schema: A strict Pydantic model applied to every received message, independently of the checks made at the handshake.
key_terms.Close code: A numeric reason sent when closing a WebSocket: 1000 for normal completion, 1008 for a policy violation and 1009 for a message too big.

worked_examples.title: a receive loop that ends on disconnect
worked_examples.interpretation: The lesson's handler reads one message and closes, while most real sockets run a loop like this one until the client leaves. There is no special return value for a closed connection: `receive_text` raises `WebSocketDisconnect`, carrying the close code the client sent, here 1001 for going away. Catching that exception is the normal exit path, not an error, and the `finally` block is where per connection state such as chat room membership or a subscription to a message broker must be released. "ALTER TABLE note ADD COLUMN category VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL",
"ALTER TABLE note ADD COLUMN category VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'general'",

title: Django QuerySets, aggregation and evaluation

key_terms.QuerySet: A Django object describing a database query that is built by methods such as filter and order_by and run only when evaluated.
key_terms.Lazy evaluation: Deferring SQL execution until results are needed, for example by iteration or list conversion, after which that QuerySet caches its rows.

worked_examples.title: where a filter sits decides WHERE or HAVING

"SELECT region, SUM(amount), COUNT(id) FROM sale WHERE amount >= 3 "
"GROUP BY region HAVING SUM(amount) >= 3 ORDER BY region"
worked_examples.interpretation: These two statements are the shapes Django builds for two chains that read almost the same. `Sale.objects.filter(amount__gte=3).values("region").annotate(total=Sum("amount"))` filters rows before grouping, so the south sale of 2 vanishes and south reports a total of 4 from one row. Moving the condition after the annotation, as in `.annotate(total=Sum("amount")).filter(total__gte=3)`, filters finished groups with HAVING, so south keeps both sales and totals 6. Neither is wrong, but a report that silently changes its counts when someone reorders a chain is a real bug. key_terms.select_related: A QuerySet method that follows single-valued relationships with a SQL join and builds the related objects from the same rows.

Python searches the method resolution order from left to right, so `Guarded` reaches `GuardMixin.dispatch` first, and the mixin hands off to `View` through `super()` only after the header check passes. In `Unguarded` the base view's `dispatch` answers first and never calls `super()`, so the guard is dead code and the request with no key gets a 200. The last line shows why a per-user salt matters: the same password gives a different value, so equal hashes do not reveal equal passwords. worked_examples.title: why every CSRF token differs but all validate

That is why the lesson can fetch `/token/` once and reuse the value, and why a missing header still gets 403.
