key_terms.Owner-scoped list: A collection query filtered by `request.user`, so each user sees only the notes that user created.
key_terms.Trusted owner assignment: Setting the owner from `request.user` after `commit=False`, while an `owner` key in the POST is refused with 400.
key_terms.CSRF-enforcing client: A test Client created with `enforce_csrf_checks=True`, so a POST without a token receives 403 as it would in a browser flow.
key_terms.Row-count check: Counting stored rows after the requests to prove that refused writes left no record behind.

worked_examples.title: a strict key check still sees repeated keys as one
worked_examples.interpretation: The lesson's view refuses any body where `set(request.POST) != {"title"}`, which turns a forged `owner` field into a 400 before the form runs. Form data can repeat a key, though, and a set of keys hides that: the third body passes the check with two titles. Django's `QueryDict` returns the last value for `request.POST["title"]`, so `Second` would be saved. If duplicates should be errors, compare `len(request.POST.getlist("title"))` as well.

title: Structured concurrency and service time budgets
outcome: Bound related async operations, propagate failures and distinguish application deadlines from client timeouts.

key_terms.Structured concurrency: Keeping child tasks inside a parent scope that does not exit until every child has finished or been cancelled.
key_terms.TaskGroup: The asyncio context manager that owns the tasks created in it and cancels the remaining ones when one task fails.
key_terms.ExceptionGroup: An exception that carries several task failures together and is handled selectively with `except*`.
key_terms.asyncio.timeout: A context manager that cancels the work inside it when a deadline passes and raises TimeoutError at the context boundary.
key_terms.Deadline budget: The total time allowed for a request, which must cover queueing, dependency calls, retries, cleanup and the response.

worked_examples.title: gather leaves a sibling running, TaskGroup cancels it
worked_examples.interpretation: With `asyncio.gather`, the first exception propagates to the caller at once, but the slow sibling keeps running in the background and finishes after the request has already failed. In a web handler that means work, connections and possibly writes outliving the response that reported an error. The `TaskGroup` version cancels the sibling, waits for its `finally` or `except` cleanup, and only then raises the `ExceptionGroup` that `except*` unpacks. That ordering is what the lesson asserts with its `cleaned` event: the caller sees the failure only after every child has stopped.

title: Retries, idempotency and transactional outboxes
outcome: Implement a small atomic outbox/identity case and explain retry-safe effects under uncertain delivery.

key_terms.Transactional outbox: A table written in the same transaction as the business change, so the change and its notification intent commit or roll back together.
key_terms.Dispatcher: A separate process that reads outbox entries and delivers them, retrying when delivery is not confirmed.
key_terms.At-least-once delivery: A guarantee that a message is delivered one or more times, because a lost acknowledgement leads to a retry.
key_terms.Idempotent consumer: A receiver that records each event identity with its effect, here with `INSERT OR IGNORE`, so a repeated delivery changes nothing.

worked_examples.title: a capped backoff schedule that respects a deadline
worked_examples.interpretation: Each delay doubles until the two second cap, and the loop stops before the total wait would pass the caller's budget, so eight permitted attempts shrink to five under a five second deadline and to three under one second. In production each ceiling would be the upper bound of a random full jitter delay, so many clients do not retry in lockstep. A schedule only makes retries polite; it does not make them safe. They are safe in the lesson because `accept` looks up the order identifier first and returns `replayed` instead of inserting a second order.

title: Database performance, indexes and contention
outcome: Inspect real bounded query plans and transaction conflicts, then map the limits of SQLite evidence to PostgreSQL.

key_terms.Composite index: An index on several columns in a fixed order, such as owner then id, that supports filters and ordering in that sequence.
key_terms.EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN: The SQLite statement that describes the strategy chosen for a query, such as a scan or a search using a named index.
key_terms.Keyset pagination: Fetching the next page with a predicate such as `id > ?` and an ORDER BY instead of a growing OFFSET.
key_terms.Write lock: The exclusive lock taken by `BEGIN IMMEDIATE`, which makes a competing writer fail with a database is locked error until rollback or commit.

worked_examples.title: offset pages repeat a row after an insert, keyset pages do not
code: db.execute("CREATE TABLE notes (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, title TEXT)")
db.executemany("INSERT INTO notes (title) VALUES (?)", [(str(i),) for i in range(1, 7)])
page_one = [r[0] for r in db.execute("SELECT id FROM notes ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 2")]
by_offset = [r[0] for r in db.execute("SELECT id FROM notes ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 2 OFFSET 2")]
"SELECT id FROM notes WHERE id < ? ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 2", (page_one[-1],)
worked_examples.interpretation: A reader fetched the newest two notes, then a write added note 7 before the second page. Counting with `OFFSET 2` now lands one row earlier, so note 5 appears twice and a busy list can also skip rows when deletes happen. The keyset query carries the last id seen and asks for ids below it, so the page is defined by data rather than position. It also scales better: with the lesson's `notes(owner, id)` index, `WHERE owner = ? AND id > ?` seeks straight to the boundary, while a large offset still walks and discards every earlier row.

title: Caching, rate limits and worker coordination
outcome: Compare cache/invalidation and per-process coordination with the explicit shared-state workshop contract.

key_terms.Cache key dimensions: The inputs, such as tenant and representation version, that must be in a cache key so one entry is never served for another.
key_terms.Token bucket: A rate limiter that holds up to a capacity of tokens, refills them at a fixed rate and spends one per admitted request.
key_terms.Refill rate: The number of tokens added per second, capped at the bucket's capacity.
key_terms.Monotonic clock: A clock that never moves backward, used for elapsed time so wall-clock adjustments cannot distort the refill.
key_terms.Global quota: A limit shared by every worker, which needs shared atomic state because one bucket per process grants each worker its own budget.

worked_examples.title: read then write admits twice, one conditional update admits once
code: db.execute("CREATE TABLE quota (key TEXT PRIMARY KEY, remaining INTEGER)")
sql = "UPDATE quota SET remaining = remaining - 1 WHERE key = ? AND remaining > 0"
print([take(), take()], db.execute("SELECT remaining FROM quota").fetchone()[0])
worked_examples.interpretation: The first half interleaves two workers the way real processes can: both read one remaining request, both decide to admit, and both write zero. The quota ends at zero and looks correct, yet two requests got through. The second half moves the check into the write itself, so the store decides and `rowcount` reports whether this caller won. This is the shared, atomic coordination the lesson's return value says a distributed limit needs; its in-process `Bucket` objects cannot provide it, since `worker_b` admits a request after `worker_a` has refused one.

title: Logs, metrics and tracing without sensitive payloads
outcome: Record useful request diagnostics with bounded labels and an actual in-memory tracing exporter.

key_terms.Span: One timed operation in a trace, with attributes such as `http.route` and the response status code.
key_terms.Metric label: A dimension on a metric such as a Prometheus counter; every distinct label combination creates a separate time series.
key_terms.Cardinality: The number of distinct label values; using the route pattern instead of the literal path keeps it bounded.
key_terms.Route pattern: The template a request matched, such as `/notes/{identifier}`, with one fixed fallback label for unmatched requests.
key_terms.Sensitive-data exclusion: Keeping values such as the Authorization header and query string out of logs, metrics and span attributes.

worked_examples.title: labeling by raw path leaks secrets and multiplies series
code: by_route = Counter(route_of(target) for target in requests)
print(len(raw), any("token" in label for label in raw))
worked_examples.interpretation: Using the request target as a metric label creates one time series per distinct URL, and the query string carries the token straight into the metrics store. Labeling by route template collapses the three note requests into one series and files the 404 under `unmatched`, exactly the values the lesson's middleware reads from `request.scope["route"].path`. Every new identifier would otherwise grow the Prometheus registry without bound. The same rule keeps the log line and the `http.route` span attribute free of `/notes/7` and the token.

title: Network streaming, backpressure and disconnects
outcome: Reproduce actual workshop HTTP/WS/SSE behavior and separate wire timing from in-process test-client buffering.

key_terms.Buffering: Holding streamed output in a client, server or proxy before forwarding it, which can delay events even when the generator is correct.
key_terms.Delivery-order test: Waiting for an actual queued or running event before releasing the held job, which proves bytes arrived before completion.
key_terms.Connection lifetime: The span of one HTTP stream; closing it does not cancel or take ownership of the durable job it reports on.
key_terms.Job-scoped cursor: A resume position that refers to persistent event rows of the selected job, so reconnecting cannot read another job's events.

worked_examples.title: a bounded queue makes a fast producer wait
code: while (chunk := await queue.get()) is not None:
worked_examples.interpretation: The producer could generate all six chunks instantly, but `put` suspends whenever two items are waiting, so memory held between the stages never exceeds two chunks while the slow consumer catches up. That suspension is backpressure: the slowest party sets the pace. An unbounded queue would accept everything and grow with every slow client. In a streaming endpoint the consumer is the network socket, and awaiting the send or drain step plays the role of the full queue. When the client disconnects, that await is where cancellation arrives.

title: Web threat modeling, proxies and TLS boundaries
outcome: Evaluate concrete input, origin, forwarding and secret-handling threats in the owned application design.

key_terms.Reverse proxy: A server in front of the application that can terminate TLS and forward requests to it over another connection.
key_terms.X-Forwarded-Proto: A header describing the scheme of the original request, trustworthy only when a trusted proxy set or sanitized it.
key_terms.ProxyFix: Werkzeug middleware that applies forwarded values for a configured number of trusted hops per field, here `x_proto=1` and `x_host=0`.
key_terms.TrustedHostMiddleware: Starlette middleware that refuses requests whose Host header is not on the allowed list, here with 400.
key_terms.TLS termination: Ending the encrypted HTTPS connection at a proxy, which then forwards the request over a separate connection.

worked_examples.title: which X-Forwarded-For entry to believe
worked_examples.interpretation: The client sent a forged `X-Forwarded-For: 6.6.6.6`, and the one real proxy at 10.0.0.2 appended the address it actually saw. Reading the leftmost entry trusts the attacker. Counting back one hop from the connected peer gives 203.0.113.9, which is what Werkzeug's `ProxyFix(x_for=1)` does. Claiming two hops when only one proxy exists hands the choice back to the client. The lesson applies the same reasoning to `x_proto=1`: the count must match the real deployment, and the app must not be reachable without passing through that proxy.

title: Container deployment, migrations and recovery
outcome: Build, start, stop and resume the owned web application with persistent data and source-bound acceptance.

key_terms.Image: A prepared, read-only package of code and dependencies from which containers are created.
key_terms.Container: A running or stopped process instance created from an image, with its own lifecycle separate from the image.
key_terms.Named volume: Docker-managed storage, here holding PostgreSQL data, that persists when application containers are replaced.
key_terms.Resume versus replace: Resume restarts the exact existing containers; replace recreates the application containers from the saved image while keeping the database volume.
key_terms.Migration step: Applying reviewed schema migrations as an explicit start action rather than on every resume or inside a request.

worked_examples.title: an added column breaks positional reads in old code
code: db.execute("CREATE TABLE note (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, title TEXT)")
return db.execute("SELECT id, title FROM note").fetchall()
db.execute("ALTER TABLE note ADD COLUMN owner TEXT")
worked_examples.interpretation: During a rolling replacement the migration runs while containers with the old image are still serving. Adding a nullable column is the expand step, and it is compatible only with code that names its columns: the explicit query still returns the prior record, while the `SELECT *` unpacking fails on the third column. The schema version moved to 2 in the same database the old process reads, which is why a migration must be safe for both images at once. Dropping or renaming the old column waits for a later release, after no old container remains.

title: Integration, failure and load testing
outcome: Combine real framework tests with explicit service-level failure/load probes and interpret their scope.

key_terms.Test isolation: Giving each test its own fresh application and state so results do not depend on the order tests run in.
key_terms.Boundary value: An input at or just beyond an accepted limit, such as quantity 0, 1, 5 or 6, which is where validation errors usually hide.
key_terms.subTest: A unittest context manager that reports each related input separately so a failure names the exact value.
key_terms.Side-effect assertion: Checking stored effects after a request, since a status code alone cannot prove that a refused request changed nothing.
key_terms.Dependency failure: A simulated unavailable dependency that returns 503 before any effect, followed by a check that the service recovers.

worked_examples.title: lax coercion accepts values the strict contract refuses
code: from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict, Field, ValidationError
worked_examples.interpretation: In lax mode pydantic converts the string `"2"`, the float `2.0` and even `True`, which becomes a reservation of quantity 1. The lesson's `Input` model sets `strict=True`, and its `test_invalid_values_have_no_effect` case lists `True` and `"2"` for this reason: a boundary test that only tried 0 and 6 would pass against either model and miss the coercion. Running each value inside `subTest` lets one failing input be reported without hiding the others, and checking `self.effects` afterward proves that a 422 also left no side effect.

title: End-to-end Python web engineering review
outcome: Choose and defend a framework architecture, reproduce a complete request/job flow and diagnose an intentional failure without losing state.

key_terms.WSGI: The synchronous Python web server interface that Flask is built on, in which one call handles one request.
key_terms.ASGI: The asynchronous Python server interface that FastAPI uses, which also supports long-lived connections such as WebSockets.
key_terms.Integrated framework: A framework such as Django that ships its own ORM, migrations, authentication, forms and admin.
key_terms.Ownership map: A record of which component owns each piece of state: the database owns jobs, the worker owns progress and the browser owns its connection.

worked_examples.title: the layer that refuses each request in the note flow
code: visible = [n["title"] for n in notes if n["owner"] == request["user"]]
worked_examples.interpretation: Each request is stopped by a different boundary, and the second value names it, which is the habit the review asks for when the integrated flow fails: say which layer decided. The order matters too. The CSRF check runs before input validation, so a cross site page learns nothing about which fields the form accepts, and the owner comes from the session, never the body. Bob's collection read returns an empty list rather than Alice's note because the listing applies the same owner scope as storage. Map each line to the framework you choose: Flask, FastAPI and Django all have a distinct place for every one of these decisions.
